questions.prompt: Match each sound source to the part that vibrates.
Where is the human voice produced?
options: In the larynx (voice box), by vibrating vocal cords
questions.explain: Air from the lungs makes the vocal cords in the larynx vibrate.

questions.prompt: In the Vibration Lab, what happened when the ruler's overhang was made SHORTER?
options: It vibrated more slowly and the pitch went down
It vibrated faster and the pitch went up
questions.explain: A shorter vibrating part vibrates faster: higher frequency, higher pitch.

questions.prompt: A tuning fork vibrates 256 times per second. What is its frequency?
questions.explain: Frequency = number of vibrations per second, in hertz.

questions.prompt: A mosquito's wings beat 3000 times in 5 seconds. What is the frequency of the buzz?
How could you show that a sounding tuning fork is vibrating? Choose all that apply.
options: Touch it gently to the surface of water and watch the splashes
Hang a table-tennis ball touching it and watch it bounce away
Touch it lightly and feel the tingle
questions.explain: Vibrations are often too fast to see, but their effects can be seen and felt.

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation to find how the length of a ruler hanging over a desk affects the pitch of its twang.
questions.modelAnswer: Independent variable: overhang length (10, 14, 18, 22, 26 cm). Dependent variable: pitch, measured as frequency with a free phone tuner or sound-analyser app. Control variables: the same ruler, clamped firmly with the same weight, flicked with the same force, in the same quiet room. Repeat each length three times and average. Plot frequency against length.
rubric: Dependent variable: pitch/frequency and how it is measured
questions.explain: Criterion B: plan a fair, measurable test.
